seo.shortDescription: Searchable U.S. duty table for all 136 HTS Chapter 74 copper lines: copper wire, rod, sheet, foil, tube and fittings pay the 50% Section 232 copper tariff on full value from every country (China 75%); refined copper cathode, scrap and other unwrought copper are outside it.

overview.intro:
Chapter 74 covers copper from the smelter to the finished article: copper mattes, unrefined copper, **refined copper cathode** and unwrought alloys, **scrap** and master alloys (7401–7405), and the semi-finished and fabricated products made from them: powders, bars and rods, **wire**, plates, sheet and strip, **foil**, **tubes and pipes**, fittings, stranded wire, fasteners, household ware and other articles of copper and brass (7406–7419). Base rates are low: Free to 3%.

What decides the cost is **Section 232**. Every line of 7406–7419 (113 of the 136 lines) pays **an extra 50% of its full customs value** from every country (heading 9903.82.02): Chile, Canada, Mexico, Peru, Germany, Japan and Korea included, and with no lower rate for the UK. FTA and USMCA claims do not reduce it. Since April 6, 2026 the duty is charged on the full value; from August 1, 2025 it applied only to the copper content. **Refined copper cathode, unwrought copper and alloys, mattes, scrap and master alloys (7401–7405) are outside Section 232** and also on the 2026 Section 301 exemption list, so they pay their base rate only (Free or 1%, and Free under the Chile, Peru and USMCA agreements). China pays another **25%** under Section 301 on almost everything.

Antidumping and countervailing duties also apply to seamless copper pipe and tube, brass sheet and strip, brass rod and phosphor copper from named countries. They are company-specific and not part of this table or the tariff calculator; see Tariff updates.

productGroups.label: Copper mattes & cement copper
productGroups.blurb: Copper mattes and cement copper (precipitated copper), the intermediate products of smelting: 1 line, Free. Outside Section 232 and on the 2026 Section 301 exemption list; not on any China Section 301 list.

productGroups.label: Unrefined copper & anodes
productGroups.blurb: Unrefined copper, including blister copper and copper anodes for electrolytic refining: 1 line, Free. Outside Section 232; China pays 25% (List 3).

productGroups.label: Refined copper & alloys, unwrought (cathode)
productGroups.blurb: Refined copper cathodes, wire bars, billets and unwrought brass, bronze and other copper alloys: 8 lines at 1%, Free under the Chile, Peru, USMCA and other FTAs. Outside Section 232: the 50% copper tariff does not apply to cathode.

productGroups.label: Copper waste & scrap
productGroups.blurb: Copper and copper-alloy waste and scrap, including brass and bronze scrap and spent anodes: 10 lines, all Free. Outside Section 232 and on the 2026 Section 301 exemption list; only China (25%) and Russia pay extra.

productGroups.label: Master alloys of copper
productGroups.blurb: Copper master alloys used as additives, such as phosphor copper and beryllium copper master alloy: 3 lines, Free. Outside Section 232; phosphor copper from Korea is under an antidumping order.

productGroups.label: Copper powders & flakes
productGroups.blurb: Copper powders of non-lamellar and lamellar structure, and flakes: 2 lines, Free; +50% Section 232.

productGroups.label: Copper bars, rods & profiles
productGroups.blurb: Bars, rods and profiles (including hollow profiles) of refined copper, brass, cupro-nickel and other alloys: 15 lines at 1% to 3%; +50% Section 232. Brass rod from seven countries is under AD/CVD orders.

productGroups.label: Copper wire
productGroups.blurb: Copper wire of refined copper (including wire rod over 9.5 mm), brass, cupro-nickel and other alloys, bare or plated: 9 lines at 1% or 3%; +50% Section 232. Insulated wire and cable are heading 8544, not Chapter 74.

productGroups.label: Copper plates, sheets & strip
productGroups.blurb: Copper plates, sheets and strip over 0.15 mm thick, of refined copper, brass, bronze, cupro-nickel, nickel silver and beryllium copper: 26 lines at 1% to 3%; +50% Section 232. Brass sheet and strip from France, Germany, Italy and Japan is under AD orders.

productGroups.label: Copper foil & copper-clad laminates
productGroups.blurb: Copper foil not over 0.15 mm thick, backed or not, including copper-clad laminates for printed circuit boards: 8 lines at 1% to 3%; +50% Section 232.

productGroups.label: Copper tubes & pipes
productGroups.blurb: Tubes and pipes of refined copper (seamless plumbing and ACR tube), brass, cupro-nickel and other alloys: 8 lines at 1.4% to 3%; +50% Section 232. Seamless refined copper pipe and tube from China, Mexico and Vietnam is under AD orders.

productGroups.label: Copper tube & pipe fittings
productGroups.blurb: Copper and brass tube or pipe fittings such as couplings, elbows, sleeves and nipples, threaded or not: 8 lines at 3%; +50% Section 232.

productGroups.label: Stranded wire, cables & plaited bands
productGroups.blurb: Stranded copper wire, cables and plaited bands, not electrically insulated, with or without fittings: 3 lines at 2% or 3%; +50% Section 232.

productGroups.label: Copper nails, screws, bolts & washers
productGroups.blurb: Nails, tacks, staples, washers, rivets, screws, bolts and nuts of copper or brass: 8 lines at 1.4% to 3%; +50% Section 232.

productGroups.label: Household & sanitary ware of copper
productGroups.blurb: Table, kitchen and household articles of copper (cookware, pot scourers) and sanitary ware: 11 lines at 3%; +50% Section 232. Chinese household articles (7418.10) pay 7.5% under List 4A instead of 25%.

productGroups.label: Other articles of copper
productGroups.blurb: Other articles of copper: cast or forged brass plumbing goods, copper wire cloth and Fourdrinier wires, springs, chain and other articles: 12 lines, Free or 3%; +50% Section 232.

workedExamples.title: $1,000,000 of copper cathode from Chile
workedExamples.body: Refined copper cathode is **outside Section 232**: Proclamation 10962 and note 16(c)(v) list only 7406–7419. Its 1% base rate is **Free** under the U.S.–Chile FTA (CL), and 7403.11 is on the 2026 Section 301 exemption list (note 52(b)), so the duty is **$0**. Without an FTA claim the base rate is $10,000.

workedExamples.title: Copper wire rod from Canada, with a USMCA certification
workedExamples.body: Refined copper wire with a cross-section over 9.5 mm (wire rod) is 1%, and USMCA makes it Free, but it is a Section 232 copper article, so it pays **+50% of its full value** (9903.82.02): **$50,000 on $100,000**. Note 16(b) collects the duty on top of any FTA rate, there is no Canada exemption, and Canada's Section 338 duty does not reach Chapter 74.

workedExamples.title: Seamless copper tube from Mexico
workedExamples.body: 1.5% base (Free with USMCA) **+ 50%** Section 232 (9903.82.02): 50% with a USMCA claim, 51.5% without. Seamless refined copper pipe and tube from Mexico is also under a 2010 antidumping order (continued in 2022), so the exporter's cash-deposit rate is added on top.

workedExamples.title: Brass sheet from China
workedExamples.body: 1.9% base **+ 50%** Section 232 (9903.82.02) **+ 25%** Section 301 List 3 (9903.88.03) = **76.9%**: $76,900 on $100,000. The 12.5% 2026 Section 301 duty on China does not apply to Section 232 goods (note 52(f)(1)).

workedExamples.title: Copper scrap from Mexico or Canada
workedExamples.body: Refined copper scrap is **Free**, outside Section 232 and on the 2026 Section 301 exemption list (9903.05.86), so it pays **no duty**, with or without a USMCA claim. Chinese copper scrap pays 25% (List 3).

workedExamples.title: Copper-clad laminate from South Korea, before and after April 6, 2026
workedExamples.body: 3% base, Free under KORUS. From August 1, 2025 the 50% copper duty applied only to the **value of the copper content** (9903.78.01; the non-copper content went under 9903.78.02 at 0%). Since **April 6, 2026** it applies to the **full customs value** (9903.82.02): a $100,000 laminate whose copper is worth $30,000 paid $15,000 and now pays $50,000.

notes.chapterNotes:
**Note 1 (definitions).** (a) *Refined copper*: metal with at least 99.85% copper by weight, or at least 97.5% copper when no other element exceeds its limit in the note's table (for example silver 0.25%, arsenic 0.5%, lead 1.5%, tin 0.8%, zinc 1%; other elements 0.3% each). (b) *Copper alloys*: metallic substances other than unrefined copper in which copper predominates by weight over each other element, provided at least one other element exceeds its table limit or the other elements total more than 2.5%. (c) *Master alloys*: alloys with more than 10% copper, not usefully malleable, used as additives, deoxidants or desulfurizing agents in nonferrous metallurgy; copper phosphide (phosphor copper) with more than 15% phosphorus is heading 2853.

**Subheading note 1.** Defines copper-zinc base alloys (*brasses*; zinc predominates over other elements, nickel under 5%, tin under 3%), copper-tin base alloys (*bronzes*), copper-nickel-zinc base alloys (*nickel silvers*; 5% or more nickel) and copper-nickel base alloys (not more than 1% zinc).

seo.shortDescription: Every change to U.S. tariffs on copper (HTS Chapter 74) since January 2025, with official sources: the 50% Section 232 copper tariff (August 1, 2025), its move to full customs value (April 6, 2026), the cathode and scrap exemptions, China Section 301, the end of the IEEPA tariffs and the copper pipe and brass AD/CVD orders.

tariffUpdates.intro:
This page compares two editions of the tariff schedule, the **2025 Basic Edition** (in force January 1, 2025) and the current **2026 Revision 21** (in force October 9, 2026), and lists every extra duty that reaches Chapter 74 today. Base rates did not change: all 136 lines carry the same general rate in both editions.

The extra duties changed completely. In January 2025 copper paid no Section 232 duty. **Proclamation 10962** put a **50%** duty on semi-finished copper and copper-intensive derivatives from **August 1, 2025** (heading 9903.78.01), charged on the **value of the copper content** only, with refined cathode, ores, concentrates, mattes and scrap left out. **Proclamation 11021** moved copper into the combined metals program on **April 6, 2026** (heading 9903.82.02) and charges the 50% on the **full customs value**. The IEEPA tariffs ended on **February 24, 2026**; neither the Section 122 surcharge nor the 2026 Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies charge any Chapter 74 line. China's Section 301 duty (25%, or 7.5% on household ware) still stacks.

Antidumping and countervailing duty orders cover copper pipe and tube, brass sheet and strip, brass rod and phosphor copper. They are company-specific, listed below for reference, and **not included in the tariff calculator**.
tariffUpdates.scope: Chapter 99 measures that reach Chapter 74 from any country: Section 232 copper (note 16; note 36 in the 2026 Basic Edition), China Section 301 (note 20), the 2026 Section 301 actions on 60 economies and Brazil (notes 50, 52), Russia's rates in lieu of column 2 (note 30), the scheduled Nicaragua Section 301 duty (note 29), and the ended IEEPA and Section 122 duties. Canada's Section 338 lists (note 51) contain no Chapter 74 line. The antidumping and countervailing duty orders on Chapter 74 products are listed for reference; the calculator does not model them. For the rate each supplier pays, see Rates by country.

There are no country exemptions: the UK's lower rates (9903.82.04, .05) are only for aluminum and steel, and the 10% rate for U.S.-smelted copper (9903.82.06) applies to derivative articles and insulated copper wire (8544), not to Chapter 74 articles. changes.title: No Chapter 74 base-rate changes
changes.detail: All 136 Chapter 74 lines carry the same general rate in the 2026 Revision 21 as in the 2025 Basic Edition; none changed and none are new or renumbered.

changes.title: Section 301 tariff on Nicaragua phases in from 2027
changes.detail: Products of Nicaragua that are not CAFTA-DR originating goods will pay +10% from January 1, 2027 and +15% from January 1, 2028 (9903.89.01, U.S. note 29). The rate is 0% in 2026.

changes.title: China Section 301 duties continue during the review
changes.detail: USTR announced that the 2018–2019 Section 301 actions on China, including List 3 (25%) and List 4A (7.5%) that cover 135 Chapter 74 lines, continue while the statutory four-year review proceeds.

changes.title: Copper pipe and tube from Mexico: preliminary review results
changes.detail: Commerce published preliminary results of the 2024–2025 administrative review of the antidumping order on seamless refined copper pipe and tube from Mexico (7411.10.10), which sets company-specific cash-deposit rates when final.

changes.title: Brass rod: preliminary review results for Korea, Brazil and South Africa
changes.detail: Commerce published preliminary results of the first administrative reviews of the brass rod orders: antidumping on Korea (September 14), Brazil (September 8) and South Africa (September 3), and countervailing on Korea (September 10). The ITC is reconsidering its injury determination on brass rod from Israel on a court remand (July 17, 2026); the Israel orders stay in force meanwhile.

changes.title: Canada Section 338 duties: no Chapter 74 line
changes.detail: Proclamations 11046–11048 put a 50% duty (9903.03.12–9903.03.14) on Canadian products in the note 51(b) lists from August 22, 2026, with lists changed from September 15, 2026 (Proclamation 11065 for the motor-vehicle list). No Chapter 74 line is on any of the lists, so Canadian copper pays only the Section 232 duty (on 7406–7419) and its base rate.

changes.title: Commerce proposes 14 more metals derivatives; none in Chapter 74
changes.detail: Under the rolling inclusion authority of Proclamation 11021, Commerce asked for comments (by August 27, 2026) on adding 14 derivative articles to the Section 232 metals duties, including insulated copper electric conductor cables (8544.49, 8544.60) and brass-wind instruments. No Chapter 74 line is affected: all of 7406–7419 is already covered.

changes.title: 2026 Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies: no Chapter 74 line pays them
changes.detail: The 10% or 12.5% duties on goods of 60 economies (9903.05.20–9903.05.84) took effect. All of 7401–7405 is on the general exemption list (note 52(b)) and 7406–7419 pays Section 232 instead (note 52(f)(1)), so no Chapter 74 line is charged.

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge expired
changes.detail: The 10% surcharge on products of all countries (9903.03.01) expired at the close of July 23, 2026. It charged no Chapter 74 line: Section 232 copper was outside it (Proclamation 11012), and 7401–7405 were on its product exemption list (9903.03.03).

changes.title: Section 301 tariff on Brazil: no Chapter 74 line pays it
changes.detail: The 25% duty on goods of Brazil (9903.05.01) took effect. 7401–7405 are on its exemption list (note 50(a)(ii)) and Section 232 copper is excluded (note 50(a)(vi)(1)).

changes.title: Five-year review of the copper pipe and tube order on Vietnam
changes.detail: Commerce and the ITC started the first sunset review of the 2021 antidumping order on seamless refined copper pipe and tube from Vietnam (7411.10.10). The order stays in force while the review runs.

changes.title: Refined copper: no phased duty proclaimed
changes.detail: Proclamation 10962 told Commerce to report by June 30, 2026 on U.S. copper markets so the President could decide on a phased universal duty on refined copper of 15% from January 1, 2027 and 30% from January 1, 2028, as the June 30, 2025 report recommended. No proclamation imposing it has been published in the Federal Register as of October 13, 2026; refined cathode (7403) stays outside Section 232.

changes.title: Proclamation 11032 adjusts the metals program
changes.detail: From June 8, 2026, metal content counts as U.S.-made when at least 85% (by weight) was smelted and cast, or melted and poured, in the United States, and new rates apply to some equipment derivatives. Nothing changed for Chapter 74: copper articles stay at 50%.

changes.title: Commerce corrects the Section 232 annex
changes.detail: Commerce added heading 9903.82.01 (articles on the note 16 lists that contain no aluminum, steel or copper pay no Section 232 duty) from April 6, 2026, and made other technical corrections to the HTS annex of Proclamation 11021.

changes.title: Copper moves to the full-value metals program (Proclamation 11021)
changes.detail: Proclamation 11021 replaced the copper headings 9903.78.01–.02 with 9903.82.02 (Russia 9903.82.14) and charges the 50% on the full customs value regardless of copper content. Chapter 74 coverage is unchanged (7406–7419). It ended the copper derivatives inclusion process in favor of joint Commerce–USTR inclusions, allows manufacturing drawback only for Annex I-B and III derivatives of trade-agreement partners (not Chapter 74 articles), and requires privileged foreign status in foreign-trade zones. CBP's CSMS 68253075 said it would announce when reporting the country of copper smelt and cast becomes required, listing only insulated wire (8544.42, 8544.49.10); no Chapter 74 line is on that list.

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge replaces the IEEPA tariffs; Chapter 74 outside it
changes.detail: A 10% surcharge on products of all countries (9903.03.01) applied until July 23, 2026. Proclamation 11012 excluded goods subject to Section 232, and cathode, unwrought copper, scrap and master alloys (7401–7405) were on its exemption list (9903.03.03), so no Chapter 74 line paid it.

changes.title: All IEEPA tariffs end
changes.detail: After the Supreme Court held on February 20, 2026 (Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump) that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, Executive Order 14389 ended the Canada, Mexico, China and reciprocal duties, and CBP stopped collecting them from 12:00 a.m. ET on February 24, 2026. The Section 232 copper duty is not an IEEPA duty and continued. For Chapter 74 the IEEPA duties had applied to the non-copper content of Section 232 copper goods and to goods outside the exemption lists.

changes.title: 50% Section 232 tariff on semi-finished copper (Proclamation 10962)
changes.detail: Proclamation 10962 (signed July 30, 2025) imposed a 50% duty on semi-finished copper products and intensive copper derivatives of all countries, from 12:01 a.m. EDT on August 1, 2025, under heading 9903.78.01 (U.S. note 36). The duty applied only to the value of the copper content; the non-copper content was entered under 9903.78.02 at 0% and kept paying the IEEPA duties. In Chapter 74 it covered every line of 7406–7419; refined copper cathode, ores, concentrates, mattes and scrap were not covered. No drawback; FTZ goods had to take privileged foreign status. Goods under the Section 232 auto-parts duties paid those instead.

changes.title: Reciprocal tariff: cathode and scrap exempt
changes.detail: Executive Order 14257 set the reciprocal tariffs from April 5, 2025, with an Annex II exemption list (9903.01.32) that, as printed in the current schedule, includes copper mattes, unwrought copper and cathode, scrap and master alloys (7401–7405). From August 1, 2025 the reciprocal duty did not apply to the copper content of Section 232 copper goods (note 2(v)(xii)) but did apply to their non-copper content (CSMS 65794272). Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Section 232 investigation of copper imports opens
changes.detail: Executive Order 14220 directed Commerce to investigate whether imports of copper in all forms (ores, concentrates, mattes, refined copper, alloys, scrap and derivatives) threaten national security. Commerce asked for public comments on March 13, 2025 and reported on June 30, 2025.

changes.title: IEEPA duties on Canada and Mexico
changes.detail: +25% on goods of Canada (9903.01.10) and Mexico (9903.01.01) from March 4, 2025; USMCA goods were exempted from March 7, 2025. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Brass rod from Israel: AD and CVD orders
changes.detail: Commerce issued antidumping and countervailing duty orders on brass rod from Israel (mainly 7407.21.50, 7407.21.70, 7407.21.90).

changes.title: Brass rod: AD orders on five countries, CVD on India and Korea
changes.detail: Commerce issued antidumping duty orders on brass rod from Brazil, India, Mexico, Korea and South Africa and a countervailing duty order on Korea (June 13, 2024), after the countervailing duty order on India (February 13, 2024).
changes.countries: Brazil, India, Mexico, Korea, South Africa

changes.title: Brass sheet and strip orders continued
changes.detail: After a fifth sunset review, Commerce continued the antidumping duty orders on brass sheet and strip (7409.21, 7409.29) from France, Germany, Italy and Japan.

changes.title: Phosphor copper order on Korea continued
changes.detail: Commerce continued the antidumping duty order on phosphor copper (master alloy, 7405.00.10) from Korea.

changes.title: Copper pipe and tube orders on China and Mexico continued
changes.detail: Commerce continued the 2010 antidumping duty orders on seamless refined copper pipe and tube (7411.10.10) from China and Mexico.

changes.title: Copper pipe and tube from Vietnam: AD order
changes.detail: Commerce issued an antidumping duty order on seamless refined copper pipe and tube from Vietnam (7411.10.10).

changes.title: China List 4A cut to 7.5%
changes.detail: The List 4A duty on Chinese copper household articles (7418.10), 15% from September 1, 2019, was halved to 7.5% under the Phase One agreement.

changes.title: China List 3 raised to 25%
changes.detail: The List 3 duty on Chinese copper (7402–7417, 7418.20–7419), 10% from September 24, 2018, rose to 25%.

understandIndustry.why:
U.S. imports of Chapter 74 copper were **$25.08B in 2025**, +44.4% from $17.37B in 2024 and almost three times the $9.06B of 2020. The jump was in **refined copper cathode (7403.11): $16.69B, +96%**, two-thirds of the total. Chile ($8.96B of cathode, 99% of its shipments), Canada, the Democratic Republic of the Congo ($1.81B, up from $299M), Peru, South Korea, Australia ($845M, up from $35M) and Japan shipped mostly cathode. 2025 was the year the Section 232 copper investigation opened (February 25) and the 50% duty started (August 1); the duty left cathode out.

Semis and articles (7406–7419), the goods that pay Section 232 today, were $7.37B: copper wire $1.67B (-35%; Canada $1.17B), tubes and pipes $1.23B, sheet and strip $1.16B, fittings $1.04B and bars, rods and profiles $912M. Germany (sheet, strip and fittings) and China ($155M of fittings, $120M of other articles) ship mainly semis and articles. Scrap was $808M, mainly from Canada ($378M) and Mexico ($348M). So 71% of 2025 imports by value were in forms that are outside Section 232 today.

2025 is the latest full year of U.S. trade data. Copper ores and concentrates (Chapter 26) are not included. Duty-collected figures aren't available from an official source yet.

seo.shortDescription: The total U.S. tariff on copper by country and product: 50% on copper wire, rod, sheet, foil, tube and fittings from Chile, Canada, Mexico, Peru, Germany, Japan, Korea and everywhere else; China 75% to 78%; cathode and scrap Free or 1%. USMCA and FTA claims explained.

industryAreas.intro:
Each cell is the base rate for that product group plus the extra duties for that country, minus any preference, from the current tariff schedule. For copper semis and articles (7406–7419) the answer is almost the same everywhere: **50%** plus a base rate of up to 3% (Free under an FTA or USMCA), because Section 232 has no country exemptions and is collected on top of FTA rates. China pays **75% to 78%** (Section 301 adds 25%, or 7.5% on household ware).

The raw-material groups are different: copper mattes, unrefined copper, **refined cathode**, unwrought alloys, **scrap** and master alloys (7401–7405) are outside Section 232 and exempt from the 2026 Section 301 tariffs, so they pay only their base rate (Free or 1%, Free under the Chile, Peru, USMCA and other FTAs) except from China (25%) and Russia. The table does **not** include antidumping or countervailing duties on copper pipe and tube, brass sheet and strip, brass rod and phosphor copper (see Tariff updates).

tariffEngineering.h1: HTS Chapter 74: Copper and Articles Thereof — Import Documents & Ways to Lower Duty

seo.title: Importing Copper: Section 232 Copper Entry, CSMS, Invoice Rules & Ways to Lower Duty (HTS Ch. 74) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: The rules for each HTS Chapter 74 copper line: Section 232 entry under 9903.82.02 on full value, CBP's copper CSMS guidance, the copper-content invoice statement, FTZ status, marking and AD/CVD scope, plus the legal ways to pay less: cathode and scrap outside Section 232, FTA claims, non-Chinese origin and drawback.

tariffEngineering.intro:
For copper the classification decides almost everything. A Chapter 74 line in **7406–7419** is a Section 232 copper article: report **9903.82.02** with it and pay **50% of the full customs value**, with no FTA reduction and no drawback. A line in **7401–7405** (mattes, unrefined copper, refined cathode and unwrought alloys, scrap, master alloys) is outside Section 232. The invoice must state the weight and copper content (19 CFR 141.89).

The legal ways to pay less are narrow: there are no Section 232 exclusions, quotas or country rates for copper. What remains: buying copper in a form outside Section 232 (cathode, unwrought alloy or scrap) and fabricating it in the United States, claiming an FTA or USMCA for the base rate, avoiding Chinese origin (25% Section 301), classifying correctly, and checking AD/CVD scope before you buy. Each rule and lever links to its regulation or proclamation.

levers.title: Import unwrought copper, cathode or scrap and fabricate in the United States
levers.saves: The whole 50% Section 232 duty: 7401–7405 are not on the note 16(c)(v) list
levers.appliesTo: Mattes, unrefined copper, refined cathode, wire bars, billets and unwrought alloys, scrap and master alloys (7401–7405), instead of rod, wire, sheet, foil or tube
levers.document: Mill or assay certificates and the invoice statement of copper content (19 CFR 141.89) that support the 7401–7405 classification.
levers.caveat: Only real changes in what you buy count: semis rolled, drawn or extruded abroad are 7406–7419 and pay 50%. Proclamation 10962 asked Commerce to report on a possible 15% (2027) and 30% (2028) duty on refined copper; none has been proclaimed.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 16(c)(v)

levers.title: Claim the FTA or USMCA rate for the base duty
levers.saves: The base rate: 1% on cathode and unwrought copper (7403), 1% to 3% on semis and articles
levers.appliesTo: Originating goods of Chile (CL), Peru (PE), Canada and Mexico (USMCA, S), Korea (KR), Australia, Colombia, CAFTA-DR and other FTA partners; Japan (JP) for copper foil
levers.document: The agreement's certification or proof of origin (USMCA: 19 CFR 182.12; Chile: 19 CFR 10.410; Peru: 19 CFR 10.3004), kept on file and presented when CBP asks.
levers.caveat: Note 16(b): an FTA or USMCA claim never reduces the 50% Section 232 duty. For cathode from Chile or Peru it makes the duty $0.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 16(b)

levers.title: Avoid Chinese origin
levers.saves: 25% of value (7.5% on household ware): Chinese copper pays Section 301 on top of Section 232, 75% to 78% in total, against 50% to 53% from other countries
levers.appliesTo: 135 lines, for goods of China (all but 7401)
levers.document: Mill certificates and production records showing where the product was made. Origin follows the last substantial transformation; ask CBP for a binding ruling if processing happens in more than one country.
levers.caveat: Third-country processing does not change the Section 232 rate (50% everywhere) and can be checked for AD/CVD circumvention, for example on copper pipe and tube.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 20

levers.title: Classify the copper form and alloy correctly
levers.saves: The 50% duty when a product is truly unwrought (7403, 7405) or scrap (7404), and the right base rate and AD/CVD status for brass, bronze and cupro-nickel
levers.appliesTo: All lines; most often unwrought vs wrought shapes, master alloys vs alloys, scrap vs usable semis, and brass vs other alloys
levers.document: Chemical analysis (chapter note 1 and subheading note 1 thresholds), a description of form and processing, and if unsure a CBP binding ruling.
levers.caveat: Classification follows the product, not the duty: copper sold as scrap that is usable as rod or sheet is not 7404. Insulated wire and cable are heading 8544 (Section 232 at 25% or 50% under other rules).

levers.title: Check AD/CVD scope before you buy
levers.saves: The whole antidumping or countervailing duty, when the product or producer is outside the order
levers.appliesTo: Seamless copper pipe and tube (China, Mexico, Vietnam), brass sheet and strip (France, Germany, Italy, Japan), brass rod (seven countries), phosphor copper (Korea)
levers.document: The order's written scope (it, not the HTS number, decides) and the producer's company-specific cash-deposit rate; when unsure, request a scope ruling from Commerce.
levers.caveat: A product in scope pays the cash deposit even if entered under another HTS line, on top of the 50% Section 232 duty. Rates change with each administrative review.

citations.label: Copper pipe and tube orders (87 FR 31209)

levers.title: Drawback: only for the base rate and Section 301
levers.saves: Up to 99% of the base rate and Section 301 duty on goods that are exported or used in exported products
levers.appliesTo: All lines, but not the Section 232 duty on Chapter 74 copper articles
levers.document: A drawback claim to CBP with import and export records (19 CFR part 191).
levers.caveat: Proclamation 10962 allowed no drawback of the copper duty; Proclamation 11021 allows manufacturing drawback only for Annex I-B and III derivatives of trade-agreement partners, and Chapter 74 copper articles (Annex I-A) are not among them. AD/CVD are never refundable (19 CFR 191.3(b)(3)).

faqs.question: What is the U.S. tariff on copper?
searchedAs: what is the tariff on copper
is there a tariff on copper
is there a us tariff on copper
how much is the copper tariff
is there a 50 tariff on copper
faqs.answer: 50% of the full customs value for copper semis and articles (HTS 7406–7419: rod, wire, sheet, foil, tube, fittings and other articles) from every country, under Section 232 heading 9903.82.02, on top of the base rate of Free to 3%. Refined copper cathode, unwrought copper, mattes, scrap and master alloys (7401–7405) are not covered and pay Free or 1%. Chinese copper pays another 25% under Section 301 (7.5% on household ware).

faqs.question: Is the 50% copper tariff still in effect, and when did it start?
searchedAs: is there still a tariff on copper
is there a tariff on copper right now
when does the copper tariff start
are there currently tariffs on copper
faqs.answer: Yes. Proclamation 10962 imposed the 50% Section 232 copper duty for goods entered from 12:01 a.m. EDT on August 1, 2025, then on the copper content only. Proclamation 11021 kept 50% when it moved copper to heading 9903.82.02 on the full customs value from April 6, 2026, and it is in the current tariff schedule (2026 Revision 21). The Supreme Court's February 20, 2026 ruling ended only the IEEPA tariffs; the copper duty rests on Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962.

faqs.question: Is refined copper cathode exempt from the copper tariff?
faqs.answer: Yes. Copper cathode (7403.11) and other refined and unwrought copper and alloys (7403) are not on the Section 232 list (note 16(c)(v) covers 7406–7419 only), and they are on the 2026 Section 301 exemption list. Cathode pays its 1% base rate, which is Free under the Chile, Peru, USMCA and other FTAs; Chinese cathode pays 26% and Russian cathode 70%.

faqs.question: Will refined copper get a tariff in 2027?
faqs.answer: Not so far. Commerce's June 30, 2025 report recommended a phased universal duty on refined copper of 15% from January 1, 2027 and 30% from January 1, 2028, and Proclamation 10962 asked Commerce to report by June 30, 2026 so the President could decide. No proclamation imposing it had been published in the Federal Register as of October 13, 2026.

faqs.question: Is there a tariff on copper scrap?
faqs.answer: Copper and brass scrap (heading 7404, e.g. 7404.00.30.20 refined copper scrap, 7404.00.60.55 brass scrap) is Free, outside Section 232 and on the 2026 Section 301 exemption list, so it pays no duty from Canada, Mexico or most other countries. Chinese scrap pays 25% (Section 301 List 3).

faqs.question: Is there a tariff on copper wire?
searchedAs: is there a tariff on copper wire
faqs.answer: Yes. Bare copper wire (heading 7408, 1% or 3% base) and stranded wire and cable (7413) pay the 50% Section 232 duty from every country, Canada included, with or without USMCA. Insulated wire and cable are heading 8544, outside Chapter 74; the insulated copper conductors of 8544.42 and 8544.49.10 pay 25% under Section 232 when copper is at least 15% of their weight, or 10% with at least 85% U.S.-smelted copper.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on copper pipe and tube?
faqs.answer: Seamless refined copper tube is 7411.10.10 (1.5%); other copper and brass tubes are 7411.10.50–7411.29 (1.4% to 3%) and fittings 7412 (3%). All pay +50% Section 232. Seamless refined copper pipe and tube from China, Mexico and Vietnam also carries antidumping duties, and Chinese tube pays 25% Section 301 as well.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on copper from China?
searchedAs: what is the tariff on copper from china
does the us import copper from china
faqs.answer: Chinese copper semis and articles pay the base rate + 50% Section 232 + 25% Section 301 List 3: 75% to 78%. Household ware (7418.10) pays 7.5% under List 4A instead, 60.5% in total. Cathode, scrap and other 7402–7405 goods pay 25% plus their base rate. The 12.5% 2026 Section 301 duty on China does not apply to Chapter 74.

faqs.question: Does the copper tariff apply to Canada and Mexico under USMCA?
searchedAs: does the us import copper from canada
faqs.answer: Yes. Section 232 has no Canada or Mexico exemption for copper, and note 16(b) collects it on top of the USMCA rate, so Canadian and Mexican copper wire, rod, sheet and tube pay 50%. A USMCA claim only removes the base rate. Cathode and scrap from Canada and Mexico are Free with USMCA. Canada's 2026 Section 338 duties do not cover any Chapter 74 line.

faqs.question: Does copper from Chile pay the tariff?
faqs.answer: Chilean refined cathode (7403.11) is Free under the U.S.–Chile FTA and outside Section 232, so it pays $0. Chilean copper semis and articles (7406–7419) pay the 50% Section 232 duty like every other country's; the FTA removes only the base rate.

faqs.question: Which HTS codes does the Section 232 copper tariff cover?
faqs.answer: In Chapter 74, every 8-digit line of 7406 through 7419 (113 ten-digit lines), listed in U.S. note 16(c)(v) to Chapter 99. Outside Chapter 74 the program reaches insulated copper wire (8544.42, 8544.49.10) at 25% and other derivatives under their own lists. There is no product exclusion process; Commerce and USTR can add derivatives (they proposed 14 more in August 2026, none in Chapter 74).

faqs.question: Is the copper tariff charged on the copper content or the full value?
faqs.answer: On the full value since April 6, 2026. From August 1, 2025 to April 5, 2026, CBP's CSMS 65794272 had importers report the copper content under 9903.78.01 (50%) and the non-copper content under 9903.78.02 (0%). Proclamation 11021 and CSMS 68253075 replaced that with 9903.82.02 on the full customs value, regardless of metal content.

faqs.question: Are there tariffs on brass?
faqs.answer: Brass rod, wire, sheet, tube, fittings and other brass articles (7407.21, 7408.21, 7409.21–.29, 7411.21, 7412.20, 7418, 7419) pay the 50% Section 232 copper duty plus a 1.4% to 3% base rate. Unwrought brass (7403.21) and brass scrap (7404) do not. Brass rod from seven countries and brass sheet and strip from France, Germany, Italy and Japan also carry antidumping or countervailing duties.

faqs.question: What is HTS Chapter 74?
faqs.answer: Chapter 74 of the Harmonized Tariff Schedule covers copper and articles of copper: mattes, unrefined and refined copper, unwrought alloys, scrap and master alloys (7401–7405) and powders, bars, rods, wire, sheet, foil, tubes, fittings, stranded wire, fasteners, household ware and other articles (7406–7419): 136 ten-digit lines with base rates from Free to 3%.

faqs.question: Where does the U.S. import copper from?
searchedAs: where does the us import copper from
where does the us get most of its copper
how much copper does the us import
faqs.answer: In 2025 the U.S. imported $25.08B of Chapter 74 copper products. The largest suppliers were Chile $9.01B (36%), Canada $3.88B (16%), Democratic Republic of the Congo $1.81B (7%), Peru $1.34B (5%), South Korea $1.26B (5%). Cathode, scrap and other unwrought copper (7401–7405) were $17.72B; semis and articles (7406–7419) $7.37B. Copper ores and concentrates are Chapter 26 and not included.
